messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Vance was ten years old the first time his stepfather’s hands closed around his wrists in the basement. The abuse never followed a predictable schedule, which meant Marcus learned to measure danger in shifts of light and sound. It almost always came at night, when the basement windows were black and the house settled into silence. His stepfather would drag him toward the corner where a heavy, scratchy wool blanket was stored, a texture that would bite his ankles and forearms as it was pulled over him. Sometimes, from upstairs, the muffled whimpers of his younger half-brother would filter through the floorboards, a sound that seemed to amplify the terror rather than distract from it. Marcus did not understand then why he could not simply run; he only knew that when the darkness pooled in the corners and that rough wool touched his skin, his body locked into a frantic stillness. Over the years, those nights followed him into his waking hours. By the time Marcus was fifteen, the basement’s shadowed corners had become a recurring film in his mind, looping every time he closed his eyes. The memories arrived with the weight of his stepfather’s grip, the bite of the wool, the cold air, and the echoing cries. When the sensation hit, the emotion became so dense he had to physically step away from whatever he was doing, his breath catching until the wave passed. He began to notice that people seemed to see right through him, as if the history of his body were printed on his skin. He felt less like a person and more like something handled, measured, and discarded. Along with that sense of exposure, he carried a steady certainty that harm could arrive from any direction, at any moment, from anyone he thought he knew. Now twenty-five and working as a housekeeper, Marcus’s daily route takes him through apartments where he hangs linens, strips mattresses, and vacuums hallways. The work should be straightforward, but the tactile demands have become a constant minefield. Two weeks ago, while stripping a king-sized bed in a client’s guest room, his fingers brushed against a thick, nubby wool throw left folded on the chair. The moment the fabric caught his skin, the memory replayed in full sensory reliving; the basement air returned, his wrists burned, and the sound of a child crying seemed to emanate from the ventilation grate. He dropped the sheet, his heart hammering against his ribs, and had to step out into the hallway until the physical trembling subsided. He told his supervisor he felt unwell and took the rest of the day off, a pattern that has cost him three overtime shifts this month. He has come to believe that dropping responsibilities keeps him safe. He quietly turns down assignments that require solo work in dimly lit storage rooms or late-night callouts. Marcus has also stopped answering calls after eight o’clock. He cannot bear the quiet that follows, nor the way the dark seems to press against his windows. When he needs to sleep, he keeps his bedroom door wide open and leaves a hallway light on, but he still sleeps with one eye peeled to the ceiling. He refuses to spend evenings alone in his own apartment, instead lingering in the lobby of the grocery store or sitting in the corner of a brightly lit diner until someone else walks in. He tells himself it is just caution, that it is wise to know who is in the room, but what frightens him most is the steady expectation that the floor could give way without warning. He tried to escape the rising panic by letting his mind drift into elaborate mental landscapes. The drift became a refuge he leaned into whenever work grew too loud or too close. He realized he was losing track of his own schedule, his own name, and his own rent payments. Tonight, Marcus sat on the edge of his mattress, the half-stripped sheets pooled around his ankles, and listened to the hum of his refrigerator. He had finally booked an intake appointment at a community mental health clinic, not because the memories had faded, but because he could no longer outmaneuver them. He is most afraid of the next blackout, the next rough fabric, the next cry that might pull him back into the basement, but what he is desperately hoping for is a way to sleep through the night without bracing for impact. He wants to know how to walk into a room and feel like a person who belongs there, rather than something waiting to be handled.
